title: Is One Layer Enough? Training A Single Transformer Layer Can Match Full-Parameter RL Training
hook: Full-parameter RL post-training updates every layer — but this study finds that training just ONE middle layer alone often recovers all the gains, and sometimes more.
key_points: Across 7 models (Qwen3, Qwen2.5), 3 RL algorithms (GRPO, GiGPO, Dr. GRPO), and tasks spanning math, code, and agentic decisions, training a single transformer layer often matches or beats full-parameter RL.
Introduces 'layer contribution': the fraction of full RL's improvement a single layer recovers when trained alone.
RL gains concentrate in a small subset of layers — frequently just one — rather than spreading evenly across the network.
High-contribution layers cluster in the MIDDLE of the transformer stack; layers near the input and output ends contribute far less.
Layer rankings stay strongly correlated across different datasets, tasks, model families, and RL algorithms — a consistent structural pattern, not a fluke of one setup.
content_html: RL post-training usually updates every parameter in a model, implicitly assuming every layer pulls its weight equally. This study tests that assumption directly — and finds it's mostly wrong.
extra_html:
The authors systematically train a single transformer layer at a time (freezing the rest) and compare the resulting gains to full-parameter RL, across seven models spanning Qwen3 and Qwen2.5, three RL algorithms (GRPO, GiGPO, Dr. GRPO), and tasks in math reasoning, code generation, and agentic decision-making. To quantify this, they define layer contribution — the fraction of full RL's improvement a single isolated layer recovers. Surprisingly, a single layer often recovers most of the full-parameter gain, and in some cases exceeds it.

The pattern is strikingly consistent: high-contribution layers cluster in the middle of the network, while layers near the input and output ends matter much less, and layer rankings stay correlated across datasets, tasks, model families, and RL algorithms alike. That points to RL post-training doing most of its real work in a narrow structural location inside the model, rather than distributing adaptation evenly — with obvious implications for cheaper, more targeted RL fine-tuning. Zijian Zhang, Mingyi Hong, and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

related.title: On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation
related.hook: On-policy distillation isn't a midpoint between fine-tuning and RL — it carves its own narrow path through parameter space, locking into a low-dimensional subspace early in training.

Right at the input embedding layer
